title: Activity Authoring Systems: SE to Hydra-Gen
description: I built several generations of Java/Swing activity-authoring systems used by Essential Skills content teams to turn teacher-created curriculum into production learning software. Early versions streamlined content entry, layout, formatting, media assignment, and activity configuration; the later Hydra-Gen generation allowed non-programmers to visually assemble new activity types from reusable EWidgets, configure behavior through properties and flags, save the result as a custom XML scripting language, and test activities live while editing.

sections.title: Several Generations of Authoring Tools
paragraphs: This was not one standalone Activity Builder. I created roughly three to four major generations of Java/Swing authoring tools as the Essential Skills activity engine and content architecture evolved.
Each generation improved the workflow for content creators while remaining compatible with the current engine and data model of its time.

sections.title: Early SE Activity Builders
paragraphs: The earlier builders were primarily content-entry, configuration, and formatting tools tied to the Essential Skills ISAM-based data systems.
Authors selected an activity type, entered or edited its content, configured properties and flags, assigned media, and adjusted formatting so each activity fit its content correctly on screen.

sections.title: Why Layout Had to Be Editable
paragraphs: Activities within the same type could still contain very different questions, answer lengths, images, paragraphs, and media. A layout that worked for one activity could be poor for another.
The authoring tools therefore allowed content teams to adjust formatting and placement for individual activities rather than requiring programmers to hand-tune every screen.

sections.title: From W.E.T. to Reusable Composition
paragraphs: Before Hydra-Gen, many activity types followed what we informally called W.E.T. development: Write Every Time. A programmer would build a new activity implementation whenever a sufficiently different interaction was required.
Hydra-Gen changed that model by breaking common interaction patterns into reusable EWidgets that could be combined to create new activity types.

sections.title: EWidgets as Functional Building Blocks
paragraphs: EWidgets were not simply primitive GUI controls. Each represented a reusable piece of learning behavior that could be combined with other pieces to form an activity.
A program designer could assemble an activity by combining complete functional elements rather than implementing the behavior from scratch.
items: Clickable image used to hear a sound or question

sections.title: Visual Drag-and-Drop Authoring
paragraphs: The Hydra-Gen Activity Builder introduced visual drag-and-drop composition. Designers could place and arrange EWidgets directly on the activity canvas and configure them through properties.
Any Hydra-Gen activity in any program could also be switched into drag-and-drop mode for fast visual editing and layout correction.

sections.title: Custom XML Scripting Language
paragraphs: Hydra-Gen saved authored activity definitions in a custom XML scripting language that we designed using a BNF grammar.

The XML described the arrangement and configuration of reusable EWidgets so the engine could interpret the activity definition at runtime rather than requiring a new compiled Java class for every activity.

sections.title: Content & Activity Definitions
paragraphs: Hydra-Gen separated the reusable activity definition from the curriculum content more clearly than earlier versions. The activity's visual and behavioral structure was authored in the Activity Builder, while the lesson/question content was managed through a separate editor.
Earlier generations were more tightly coupled: content entry, layout, properties, and activity-specific configuration were often part of the same authoring workflow.

sections.title: Behavior Without Programming
paragraphs: Non-programmers could change more than text and positioning. Activity-specific properties and flags controlled presentation and behavior without requiring code changes.
Depending on the activity type, properties could influence formatting, interaction rules, and data randomization.

sections.title: Media Authoring
paragraphs: Content creators could associate supporting media with activities, including audio, images, and animation assets.
Reward systems were managed separately and were not part of the Activity Builder itself.

sections.title: Live Testing
paragraphs: The Hydra-Gen generation supported live activity testing so program designers could immediately see how the activity behaved and looked while they were building it.
This shortened the iteration loop considerably compared with editing raw definitions and launching the student software separately.

sections.title: Program Designer Workflow
paragraphs: Program designers took teacher-created curriculum and converted it into complete production learning programs using these tools.

Programmers were still required when a genuinely new activity type, engine feature, or missing EWidget had to be developed, but existing capabilities could be reused and configured by the content team without additional programming.

sections.title: Used by Multiple Content Teams
paragraphs: The Activity Builders were heavily used by Essential Skills content creators over many years. I managed multiple teams of content creators who relied on these tools as part of the normal production workflow.
Authors performed their own testing while building, and the finished activities then went through the company's normal QA process.

sections.title: Production Scale
paragraphs: These authoring systems contributed directly to the large Essential Skills content library. Hundreds of activity types were created using the authoring architecture, and thousands of the platform's 50,000+ production learning activities were created, adjusted, reformatted, or maintained through these tools.

The value of the system was not just faster data entry. It shifted substantial portions of content production from programmers to curriculum and program-design teams while preserving reusable engine behavior underneath.

sections.title: Authoring Architecture as Leverage
paragraphs: The long-term goal was to stop treating every learning activity as a custom programming task. Reusable activity engines, configurable properties, visual layout tools, and eventually Hydra-Gen's EWidget composition model allowed a much larger content catalog to be maintained without a proportional increase in development effort.
